claim: The gut microbiota of laboratory fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster) consists of five species: L. plantarum (Lp), L. brevis (Lb), Acetobacter pasteurianus (Ap), A. tropicalis (At), and A. aceti (Aa).
source: We identified five species belonging to seven unique operational taxonomic units (OTUs) by clustering the sequences at 99% identity: L. plantarum (Lp), L. brevis (Lb), Acetobacter pasteurianus (Ap), A. tropicalis (At), and A. aceti (Aa) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data from 18 individual dissected guts and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Co-culturing L. plantarum with Acetobacter pasteurianus increases L. plantarum survival at rifampin concentrations above the MIC.
source: When grown with Ap, Lp survived after 24 h at rifampin concentrations above the MIC. Viable cell plating counts of Lp after growth in rifampin for 24 h normalized to the counts at the start of the experiment (t = 0, 3 × 105 and 4 × 105 CFU/mL in monoculture and co-culture, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by viable cell plating counts showing significantly higher survival in co-culture compared to monoculture at supra-MIC rifampin concentrations (Figure 1B).

claim: The MIC of rifampin for L. plantarum is 1.25 µg/mL in both monoculture and co-culture with Ap.
source: For Lp, the MIC was similar in co-culture as in monoculture (1.25 µg/mL, Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of MIC in both culture conditions shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All tested Acetobacter species (Ap, At, Ao, Ai, and Aa) protect L. plantarum from rifampin at supra-MIC concentrations.
source: Protection of Lp at supra-MIC concentrations of rifampin is elicited by all Acetobacter species tested. CFU/mL of Lp grown in monoculture (Lp) or in co-culture with Ap, At, A. orientalis (Ao), A. indonesiensis (Ai), and Aa, and then treated with 20 µg/mL rifampin for 24 h normalized to counts at the start of the experiment (t = 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements showing increased survival in co-cultures with all tested Acetobacter species (Figure 1C).

claim: The protective effect of Acetobacter on L. plantarum rifampin tolerance requires co-culturing before antibiotic exposure.
source: Ap-mediated survival of Lp at rifampin concentrations above the MIC is history-dependent, requiring co-culturing before exposure as compared with mixing. CFU/mL of Lp grown in monoculture, in co-culture with Ap (Co.), or mixed with Ap without subsequent growth in the absence of antibiotic (Mix), and treated with 20 µg/mL rifampin for 24 h normalized to counts at the start of the experiment (t = 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL data showing significantly lower survival in mixed cultures compared to co-cultures (Figure 1D).

claim: Co-culturing with Acetobacter extends the time to killing of L. plantarum under rifampin treatment.
source: The time to killing of Lp under rifampin treatment is extended in the presence of an Acetobacter. CFU/mL of Lp grown in monoculture and co-cultured with Ap, and treated with 50 µg/mL rifampin, normalized to counts at the start of the experiment (t = 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course CFU/mL measurements showing Lp survival >30 h in co-culture versus <18 h in monoculture (Figure 1E).

claim: The increased survival of L. plantarum in co-culture with Ap at supra-MIC rifampin concentrations is not due to growth under antibiotic treatment.
source: Single-cell imaging demonstrated that Ap-induced tolerance of Lp was not due to growth under rifampin treatment. Representative phase-microscopy images of Lp in monoculture and co-cultured with Ap on an MRS agar pad containing 50 µg/mL rifampin.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell imaging showing no growth in either mono- or co-cultures over 3 h (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).

claim: Co-culturing L. plantarum with Ap, At, or Ai results in increased L. plantarum cell density after 48 hours.
source: Co-culturing Lp with Ap, At, or Ai resulted in increased Lp cell density after 48 hr. Co-culturing with Ao or Aa did not significantly increase Lp cell density by 48 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements after 48 h of co-culture growth (Figure 2A).

claim: L. plantarum produces L- and D-lactate during growth.
source: As expected, the Lp monoculture accumulated L- and D-lactate to high levels (>100 mM; Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzymatic measurements of lactate in culture supernatants (Figure 2C).

claim: Acetobacter species consume lactate produced by L. plantarum in co-cultures.
source: L- and D-lactate accumulated to much higher levels in Lp monocultures than in co-cultures after 48 h of growth, suggesting that Acetobacter spp. consumed Lp-produced lactate. Lactate concentration was measured enzymatically from culture supernatants at 48 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by enzymatic measurements showing significantly lower lactate concentrations in co-cultures (<2 mM) compared to monocultures (>100 mM) (Figure 2C).

claim: The pH of L. plantarum monocultures decreases from pH 6.75 to below 4 during growth.
source: In the Lp monoculture, pH decreased from pH = 6.75 to below four during growth (Figure 2D); more precisely, we measured a final supernatant pH = 3.77 using a pH meter (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurements using BCECF fluorophore and pH meter (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Co-cultures of L. plantarum with Ap, At, and Ai show pH increase to ~7 after initial acidification.
source: Co-cultures with Ap, At, and Ai followed similar trajectories in which the pH mimicked that of the Lp monoculture for the first 20 hr, after which the pH increased up to a final value of ~7 (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course pH measurements using BCECF (Figure 2D).

claim: Intracellular pH of L. plantarum decreases in monoculture but not in co-culture with Ap.
source: Intracellular pH of Lp decreases upon entry to stationary phase in monoculture but not in co-culture with Ap. A strain of Lp containing a plasmid expressing the pH-sensitive GFP pHluorin (LppH) was grown in monoculture, co-cultured with Ap, or mixed with Ap at the start of the experiment.
evidence: The claim is supported by pHluorin fluorescence measurements over time and ratiometric measurements after 48 h (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).

claim: Low pH inhibits the growth of L. plantarum.
source: Lp growth is inhibited by low pH. Logarithm of OD (blue) and pH measured using BCECF (orange) after 48 h of growth in MRS at various starting pH values.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth measurements at various starting pH values showing lower carrying capacity at lower pH (Figure 3A).

claim: L. plantarum reduces the pH of the medium to a common final value of ~3.7 regardless of starting pH.
source: For all starting pH values, Lp cells reduced the pH to a common final value of ~3.7 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurements after 48 h of growth at various starting pH values (Figure 3A).

claim: The maximum growth rate of L. plantarum increases with increasing initial pH.
source: Maximal growth rate in MRS increases with increasing initial pH.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth rate measurements at various starting pH values (Figure 3C).

claim: Increasing the pH of spent L. plantarum culture from 3.77 to 7 allows growth.
source: Increasing the pH of a saturated, spent Lp culture from 3.77 to 7 allows growth, although not as much as fresh MRS.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth measurements in pH-adjusted spent medium (Figure 3D).

claim: Increasing the pH of an L. plantarum monoculture at 30 h from 4 to 7 leads to a shorter lag phase.
source: Increasing the pH of an Lp monoculture at t = 30 h from 4 to 7 to mimic the pH increase in Lp-Ap co-culture (top) leads to a shorter lag phase (bottom). Lag time was calculated by fitting growth curves to the Gompertz equation.
evidence: The claim is supported by lag time measurements from growth curves after pH adjustment (Figure 3E).

claim: Co-cultures of L. plantarum with Acetobacter species experience shorter lag times than L. plantarum monocultures.
source: Co-culture lag times are significantly shorter than Lp monoculture lag times. Lag times were obtained by fitting the growth curves in (A) to the Gompertz equation.
evidence: The claim is supported by lag time measurements from growth curves fitted to the Gompertz equation (Figure 4B).

claim: The shortened lag phase in L. plantarum-Ap co-cultures requires co-culturing before dilution into fresh medium.
source: Mixed Lp-Ap cultures do not experience significantly shorter lag times than Lp monocultures. Lag times were obtained by fitting the curves in (C) to the Gompertz equation.
evidence: The claim is supported by lag time measurements showing no significant difference between mixed cultures and monocultures (Figure 4D).

claim: Single-cell microscopy demonstrates that the decrease in lag phase in co-culture is due to L. plantarum cells, not Ap cells.
source: Single-cell microscopy demonstrates that a decrease in the duration of lag phase of Lp was responsible for the lag-time decrease in co-culture. Representative phase microscopy images of Lp in monoculture and co-cultured with Ap on an MRS agar pad.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell imaging showing Lp cells growing by 1 h in co-culture but not in monoculture, while Ap cells did not grow (Figure 4E,F).

claim: The duration of lag phase of L. plantarum depends on the time spent in stationary phase.
source: The duration of lag phase of bulk cultures of Lp depends on the time spent in stationary phase. Lp monocultures grown for various times from OD = 0.02, and co-cultures with Ap, were diluted into fresh medium. Lag time was calculated by fitting growth curves to the Gompertz equation.
evidence: The claim is supported by lag time measurements from cultures grown for different durations (Figure 5A).

claim: Culturing L. plantarum for a shorter time (20 h vs 48 h) leads to higher cell survival at supra-MIC rifampin concentrations.
source: Culturing Lp as a monoculture for a shorter time leads to higher cell survival. Viable cell plating counts of Lp after growth in 20 µg/mL rifampin for 24 h normalized to the counts at the start of the experiment (t = 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements showing significantly higher survival for 20 h cultures compared to 48 h cultures (Figure 5B).

claim: Neutralization of pH in stationary phase in L. plantarum monocultures is sufficient to induce rifampin tolerance.
source: Neutralization of pH in stationary phase in Lp monocultures is sufficient to induce tolerance. Increasing the pH of an Lp monoculture at t = 30 h or t = 40 h to 7 to mimic the pH increase in co-cultures of Lp with Acetobacter species (upper panel) increased cell survival (CFU/mL normalized to counts at the start of the experiment, t = 0) after treatment with 20 µg/mL rifampin for 24 h (lower panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements showing increased survival after pH neutralization at 30 h or 40 h (Figure 5C).

claim: Acidification of L. plantarum-Ap co-cultures during stationary phase sensitizes L. plantarum to rifampin.
source: Acidification of Lp co-cultures with Ap during the exponential-to-stationary phase transition or in late stationary phase sensitizes Lp to rifampin. Decreasing the pH of an Lp co-culture with Ap at t = 30 h or t = 40 h to 3.7 to mimic the pH of an Lp monoculture (upper panel) increased survival (CFU/mL normalized to counts at the start of the experiment, t = 0) after treatment with 20 µg/mL rifampin for 24 h (lower panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements showing significantly reduced survival after acidification at 30 h or 40 h (Figure 5D).

claim: The dynamics of killing in L. plantarum co-cultures with different Acetobacter species differs quantitatively according to species.
source: The dynamics of killing in Lp co-culture with Acetobacter species differs quantitatively according to species and from Lp monoculture (blue), indicating that the Acetobacter species induce rifampin tolerance to different degrees. CFU/mL of Lp in monoculture and in co-culture with Acetobacter species, and treated with 50 µg/mL rifampin, normalized to counts at the start of the experiment (t = 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course CFU/mL measurements showing distinct killing dynamics for different Acetobacter species (Figure 5E).

claim: The timing of pH change in Acetobacter co-culture predicts the extent of protection against rifampin.
source: The timing of the pH change in Acetobacter co-culture predicts the extent of protection against 50 µg/mL rifampin. Neutralization of pH in Lp monocultures at 40 h of growth (to mimic Lp+Aa co-cultures) elicits longer protection against rifampin than neutralization at 30 hr. A small increase in pH (from 3.85 to 4.5) at 30 h (to mimic Lp+Ao co-cultures) provides protection comparable to complete neutralization.
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements showing different protection levels based on timing and extent of pH change (Figure 5F).

claim: L. plantarum survival to erythromycin is higher for 48-h-old monocultures than for 20-h-old monocultures.
source: Lp survival to erythromycin is ~10 times higher after 24 h of treatment with erythromycin at supraMIC concentrations for 48-h-old monocultures of Lp than for 20-h-old Lp monocultures. Viable cell plating counts of Lp after growth in erythromycin for 24 h normalized to cell counts at the start of the experiment (t = 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements showing ~10-fold higher survival for 48 h cultures compared to 20 h cultures (Figure 5G).

claim: The MIC of erythromycin for L. plantarum is 0.078 µg/mL for both 20 h and 48 h cultures.
source: While both cultures had the same MIC in erythromycin (0.078 µg/mL, Figure 5G)
evidence: The claim is supported by MIC measurements shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Shifting the pH of an L. plantarum monoculture at 30 h to 7 increases the rate of killing by erythromycin.
source: Shifting the pH of an Lp monoculture at 30 h to 4 or 7, followed by 18 h of growth before treatment with 2 µg/mL erythromycin, mimics the survival dynamics of a 48-h-old or 20-h-old culture in stationary phase, respectively. CFU/mL of Lp monocultures were normalized to counts at the start of the experiment (t = 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course CFU/mL measurements showing increased killing rate after pH shift to 7 (Figure 5H).

claim: Rifampin is bactericidal.
source: Rifampin was the only drug for which all four species exhibited sensitivity (Supplementary file 1b) and it is bactericidal (Walsh and Wencewicz, 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Walsh and Wencewicz, 2016.

claim: Erythromycin is bacteriostatic.
source: We decided to use the ribosome-targeting macrolide erythromycin because it is bacteriostatic (in contrast to rifampin)
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in contrast to rifampin.

claim: Lactobacillus species produce lactic acid.
source: Lactobacillus spp. produce lactic acid (Makarova et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Makarova et al., 2006.

claim: Acetobacter species produce acetic acid and can oxidize lactate to carbon dioxide and water.
source: Acetobacter spp. produce acetic acid and are distinguished by their ability to oxidize lactate to carbon dioxide and water (Yamada et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yamada et al., 1997.

claim: The gut microbiota of Drosophila melanogaster consists of ~5 species predominantly from the Lactobacillus and Acetobacter genera.
source: This community consists of ~5 species predominantly from the Lactobacillus and Acetobacter genera (Wong et al., 2011) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wong et al., 2011 and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: All members of the Drosophila gut microbiota can be cultured in vitro.
source: The gut microbiota of Drosophila melanogaster fruit flies is such a low diversity assemblage in which all members can be cultured in vitro (Obadia et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Obadia et al., 2017.

claim: Antibiotic tolerance is defined as increased time to killing of the population as a whole without a change in MIC.
source: Tolerance has been defined as increased time to killing of the population as a whole (Brauner et al., 2017), as opposed to resistance (a change in the MIC), or persistence or heterotolerance whereby a subpopulation of bacteria displays increased time to killing (Balaban et al., 2019; Brauner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brauner et al., 2017, Balaban et al., 2019, and Brauner et al., 2016.

claim: Tolerance to beta lactams such as ampicillin has been observed in E. coli cultures that exhibit slow growth or a long lag phase.
source: Tolerance to beta lactams such as ampicillin has been observed in E. coli cultures that exhibit slow growth or a long lag phase (Brauner et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brauner et al., 2016.

claim: E. coli mutants with longer lag phases can be selected through experimental evolution to match the time of treatment.
source: E. coli mutants with longer lag phases can be selected through experimental evolution to match the time of treatment (Fridman et al., 2014; Levin-Reisman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fridman et al., 2014 and Levin-Reisman et al., 2017.

claim: The observed tolerance of L. plantarum to rifampin in co-culture is opposite to the previously identified mode of tolerance to ampicillin in E. coli.
source: A reduction in lag time exiting stationary phase was linked to L. plantarum tolerance to rifampicin, opposite to a previously identified mode of tolerance to ampicillin in E. coli.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the current findings with previous studies on E. coli tolerance to ampicillin.

claim: Interspecies interactions can impact antibiotic activity through alterations to bacterial physiology.
source: Interspecies interactions can impact antibiotic activity through many mechanisms, including alterations to bacterial physiology.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract.

claim: Acetobacter species counter the acidification driven by L. plantarum production of lactate.
source: By measuring key metabolites and environmental pH, we determined that Acetobacter species counter the acidification driven by L. plantarum production of lactate.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of lactate and pH in mono- and co-cultures.

claim: Shifts in pH are sufficient to modulate L. plantarum tolerance to rifampin and erythromycin.
source: Shifts in pH were sufficient to modulate L. plantarum tolerance to rifampin and the translational inhibitor erythromycin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that pH manipulation alone can alter antibiotic tolerance.

claim: Antibiotics impact gut communities in many ways, ranging from loss of diversity to evolution of multidrug-resistant pathogens.
source: In environments such as the human intestine, antibiotics impact communities in many ways, ranging from the loss of diversity (Dethlefsen et al., 2008; Jernberg et al., 2007) to the evolution of multidrug-resistant pathogens (Santajit and Indrawattana, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dethlefsen et al., 2008, Jernberg et al., 2007, and Santajit and Indrawattana, 2016.

claim: pH has been shown to drive community dynamics in an artificial laboratory system of decomposition bacteria.
source: An example of the latter is pH, which has recently been shown to drive community dynamics in an artificial laboratory system of decomposition bacteria (Ratzke and Gore, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ratzke and Gore, 2018.

claim: The exoproducts of Pseudomonas aeruginosa affect the survival of Staphylococcus aureus through changes in antibiotic uptake, cell-wall integrity, and intracellular ATP pools.
source: Previous studies have used synthetic communities to uncover the interplay between interspecies interactions and antibiotic efficacy; for example, the exoproducts of Pseudomonas aeruginosa affect the survival of Staphylococcus aureus through changes in antibiotic uptake, cell-wall integrity, and intracellular ATP pools (Radlinski et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Radlinski et al., 2017.

claim: In genetically modified communities, intracellular antibiotic degradation affords cross-species protection against chloramphenicol.
source: In genetically modified communities, intracellular antibiotic degradation affords cross-species protection against chloramphenicol (Sorg et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sorg et al., 2016.

claim: Metabolic dependencies within synthetic communities can lower the viability of bacteria when antibiotics eliminate providers of essential metabolites.
source: Additionally, metabolic dependencies within synthetic communities can lower the viability of bacteria when antibiotics eliminate providers of essential metabolites, leading to an apparent change in the MICof the dependent species (Adamowicz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Adamowicz et al., 2018.

claim: pH has been shown to affect antibiotic efficacy in monocultures.
source: For example, the intimate relationship between bacterial metabolism and environmental pH could also lead to changes in antibiotic efficacy, as previously shown in monocultures (Aagaard et al., 1991; Argemi et al., 2013; Kamberi et al., 1999; Karslake et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aagaard et al., 1991, Argemi et al., 2013, Kamberi et al., 1999, Karslake et al., 2016, and Yang et al., 2014.

claim: Tolerance can facilitate the evolution of resistance.
source: tolerance, an important and understudied aspect of antibiotic susceptibility that can be elicited by diverse mechanisms and can facilitate the evolution of resistance (Levin-Reisman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levin-Reisman et al., 2017.

claim: The stringent response is required to survive acid shock in Helicobacter pylori.
source: The stringent response is required to survive acid shock in Helicobacter pylori (Mouery et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mouery et al., 2006.

claim: The stringent response is not required to survive acid shock in Enterococcus faecalis.
source: The stringent response is required to survive acid shock in Helicobacter pylori (Mouery et al., 2006) but not in Enterococcus faecalis (Abranches et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Abranches et al., 2009.

claim: Intracellular acidification by the short-chain fatty acid propionate has been proposed to lengthen lag phase in Salmonella in vitro and in the mouse gut.
source: Intracellular acidification by the short-chain fatty acid propionate has been proposed to lengthen lag phase in Salmonella in vitro and in the mouse gut (Jacobson et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jacobson et al., 2018.

claim: Changes in intra- and extracellular pH have been shown to lead to transcriptional responses that provide cross-protection against antibiotics.
source: Changes in intra- and extracellular pH have been shown to lead to transcriptional responses that provide cross-protection against antibiotics (Komora et al., 2017; McMahon et al., 2007; O'Sullivan and Condon, 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Komora et al., 2017, McMahon et al., 2007, and O'Sullivan and Condon, 1997.

claim: Short chain fatty acids like butyrate play an important role in host physiology and health.
source: Some of these short chain fatty acids, like butyrate, have been shown to play an important role on host physiology and health (Nicholson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nicholson et al., 2012.

claim: Approximately 65% of human disease-causing genes have homologs in the Drosophila genome.
source: the fact that ~ 65% of human disease-causing genes have homologs in the Drosophila genome (Ugur et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ugur et al., 2016.

claim: The growth rates of lactic acid bacteria such as L. plantarum are affected by pH.
source: The growth rates of lactic acid bacteria such as Lp are known to be affected by pH (Stecka and Grzybowsii, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stecka and Grzybowsii, 2000.

claim: Increased time in starvation leads to changes in physiology, including an increase in the duration of lag phase.
source: Increased time in starvation leads to changes in physiology, including an increase in the duration of lag phase (Levin-Reisman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levin-Reisman et al., 2010.

claim: Rifampin has two ionizable functional groups with pKas of 1.7 and 7.9.
source: neither of the ionizable functional groups of rifampin (pKas 1.7 and 7.9 Maggi et al., 1966)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maggi et al., 1966.

claim: Erythromycin has a pKa of 8.88.
source: nor erythromycin (pKa 8.88 McFarland et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McFarland et al., 1997.

claim: BCECF has a pKa of approximately 6.98.
source: Culture pH was measured using the dual-excitation ratiometric pH indicator 2',7-bis-(2-carboxyethyl)−5-(and-6)-carboxyfluorescein, mixed isomers (BCECF, Invitrogen B1151, Lot 1831845), which has a pKa of ~6.98.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Lactate has a pKa of 3.86.
source: Since lactate is a short-chain fatty acid with a pKa of 3.86
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The pH-based mechanism underlying the tolerance of L. plantarum induced by Acetobacter species is intrinsically connected to the metabolic capacity of each species.
source: The pH-based mechanism underlying the tolerance of Lp induced by Acetobacter species is intrinsically connected to the metabolic capacity of each species, and hence is likely to be generally relevant in more complex communities.
evidence: The claim is based on the mechanistic findings of the study.

claim: The findings could have important implications for human health in the context of Lactobacillus-dominated vaginal microbiotas.
source: Moreover, these findings could have important implications for human health, for example in the context of Lactobacillus-dominated vaginal microbiotas (Boris and Barbés, 2000)
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential implications, supported by a citation to Boris and Barbés, 2000.

claim: Lactate accumulation by L. plantarum in monocultures acidifies the media, inhibiting growth during stationary phase.
source: Lactate accumulation by Lp in monocultures acidified the media, inhibiting growth during stationary phase.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements of lactate, pH, and growth in monocultures.

claim: Acetobacter-mediated lactate consumption releases growth inhibition by increasing pH, leading to a shorter L. plantarum lag while exiting stationary phase.
source: Acetobacter-mediated lactate consumption released this inhibition by increasing pH, leading to a shorter Lp lag while exiting stationary phase.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements of lactate, pH, and lag time in co-cultures.

claim: The reduced lag exiting stationary phase was correlated with the antibiotic tolerance of L. plantarum.
source: This reduced lag exiting stationary phase was correlated with the antibiotic tolerance of Lp that we observed.
evidence: The claim is based on correlation between lag time and tolerance measurements.

claim: Simple changes to the environment can drive complex physiological behaviors and antibiotic responses within bacterial communities.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that simple changes to the environment can drive complex physiological behaviors and antibiotic responses within bacterial communities.
evidence: The claim is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The mechanistic understanding of the coupling among interspecies interactions, environmental pH, and antibiotic tolerance enables future predictions of growth and the effects of antibiotics in more complex communities.
source: This mechanistic understanding of the coupling among interspecies interactions, environmental pH, and antibiotic tolerance enables future predictions of growth and the effects of antibiotics in more complex communities.
evidence: The claim is a forward-looking statement about the implications of the study's findings.

claim: L. plantarum cells are longer (2.46 ± 0.78 µm) and thinner (0.72 ± 0.12 µm) than Ap cells (1.66 ± 0.38 µm long and 0.90 ± 0.09 µm wide).
source: Lp and Ap were clearly distinguishable based on morphology (Figure 4—figure supplement 2): Lp cells are longer (2.46 ± 0.78 µm vs. 1.66 ± 0.38 µm) and thinner (0.72 ± 0.12 µm vs. 0.90 ± 0.09 µm) than Ap cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological measurements from microscopy images (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: The aspect ratio (length/width) is 3.41 ± 0.91 for L. plantarum and 1.87 ± 0.46 for Ap.
source: Therefore, we used the aspect ratio (length/width; 3.41 ± 0.91 for Lp and 1.87 ± 0.46 for Ap) to distinguish single cells from each species in co-culture.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological measurements from microscopy images.

claim: The classification of L. plantarum and Ap cells based on aspect ratio has a 10% error rate.
source: We validated this strategy on co-cultures of fluorescently tagged strains of the same two species and measured a 10% error rate in classification (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by validation experiments using fluorescently tagged strains (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).

claim: Ap shows a strong positive interaction with L. plantarum in 96-well plates.
source: Ap showed a strong (positive) interaction with Lp, whereas At, Ai, and Aa had an interaction score closer to 0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by interaction score calculations based on OD measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Only the Lp-Ao co-culture was significantly antagonistic in 96-well plates.
source: Only the Lp-Ao co-culture was significantly antagonistic (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by interaction score calculations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: In test tubes, only the Lp-Ap co-culture showed a significant positive interaction.
source: We also performed this measurement in cultures grown in test tubes, where we only observed a significant positive interaction of Lp with Ap (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by interaction score calculations from test tube cultures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: At and Ao reached lower CFU/mL in co-cultures with Lp than in monocultures.
source: At and Ao reached lower CFU/mL in co-cultures with Lp than in monocultures, while Ap, At, and Aa did not change significantly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Ap, At, and Aa CFU/mL did not change significantly in co-cultures with Lp compared to monocultures.
source: At and Ao reached lower CFU/mL in co-cultures with Lp than in monocultures, while Ap, At, and Aa did not change significantly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: L. plantarum benefits from growth with certain Acetobacter species including Ap.
source: Thus, Lp benefits from growth with certain Acetobacter species including Ap, and it has negative or neutral effects on the Acetobacter species (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is based on interaction scores and CFU/mL measurements.

claim: L. plantarum has negative or neutral effects on the Acetobacter species.
source: Thus, Lp benefits from growth with certain Acetobacter species including Ap, and it has negative or neutral effects on the Acetobacter species (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is based on interaction scores and CFU/mL measurements.

claim: A mutualism exists between L. plantarum and Ap driven by growth during stationary phase.
source: Thus, a mutualism exists between Lp and Ap driven by growth during stationary phase.
evidence: The claim is based on observations that both species benefit from co-culture during stationary phase.

claim: Ap in liquid monoculture shows little to no growth after 40 h in most replicates.
source: Interestingly, Ap in liquid monoculture showed little to no growth in most replicates after 40 h (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements over time (Figure 2B).

claim: In co-culture, Ap starts to grow after ~20 h and reaches saturation by ~40 h.
source: by contrast, in co-culture Ap started to grow after ~20 h and reached saturation by ~40 h (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements over time (Figure 2B).

claim: Ap benefits from growth as a co-culture with L. plantarum.
source: by contrast, in co-culture Ap started to grow after ~20 h and reached saturation by ~40 h (Figure 2B), indicating that Ap also benefited from growth as a co-culture.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of Ap growth in monoculture versus co-culture.

claim: L. plantarum displays a significant (~2X) increase in CFU/mL in the Lp-Ap co-culture after 30 hr that does not occur in monoculture.
source: Interestingly, after 30 hr, Lp displayed a significant (~2X) increase in CFU/mL in the Lp-Ap co-culture that did not occur in the monoculture (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements over time (Figure 2B).

claim: The increase in final yield of L. plantarum in co-culture occurs late in stationary phase.
source: indicating that the increase in final yield occurs late in stationary phase. Since this increase occurs generally (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is based on the timing of CFU/mL increase observed in Figure 2B.

claim: Lp-Ao co-culture harbors higher levels of L-lactate than any other co-culture except Lp-Aa.
source: The Lp-Ao co-culture harbored higher levels of L-lactate than any other co-culture and Lp-Aa had the highest concentration of L-lactate of the co-cultures (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzymatic measurements of L-lactate (Figure 2C).

claim: Lp-Aa co-culture has the highest concentration of L-lactate among the co-cultures.
source: The Lp-Ao co-culture harbored higher levels of L-lactate than any other co-culture and Lp-Aa had the highest concentration of L-lactate of the co-cultures (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzymatic measurements of L-lactate (Figure 2C).

claim: Aa and Ao are less efficient at consuming L-lactate than the other Acetobacter species.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Lp metabolism leads to an initial accumulation of lactate and that the Acetobacter species consume it, although Aa and Ao are less efficient at consuming L-lactate than the other species.
evidence: The claim is based on lactate measurements showing higher residual L-lactate in Aa and Ao co-cultures.

claim: For monocultures of all Acetobacter species except Ap, the medium first acidifies down to pH ~5, and then increases back to pH = 6–7.
source: For monocultures of all Acetobacter species except Ap, the medium first acidified down to pH ~5, and then increased back to pH = 6–7 (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurements over time using BCECF (Figure 2D).

claim: The Lp-Aa co-culture experiences a ~10 h delay in the pH increase compared to Lp-Ap, Lp-At, and Lp-Ai co-cultures.
source: The Lp-Aa co-culture experienced a ~ 10 h delay in the pH increase, while the co-culture with Ao showed only a slight pH increase by 48 h (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurements over time (Figure 2D).

claim: The co-culture with Ao shows only a slight pH increase by 48 h.
source: The Lp-Aa co-culture experienced a ~ 10 h delay in the pH increase, while the co-culture with Ao showed only a slight pH increase by 48 h (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurements over time (Figure 2D).

claim: The slight pH increase in the Lp-Ao co-culture is consistent with lower L-lactate consumption by Ao.
source: The slight pH increase in the Lp-Ao co-culture is consistent with lower L-lactate consumption by Ao (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation between pH dynamics and lactate consumption.

claim: Lactate metabolism dictates dramatic shifts in environmental pH that are related to physiological changes in antibiotic tolerance.
source: Thus, lactate metabolism dictates dramatic shifts in environmental pH that are related to physiological changes in antibiotic tolerance (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation between lactate metabolism, pH changes, and antibiotic tolerance.

claim: Intracellular pH of L. plantarum is significantly lower in monoculture than in co-culture with Acetobacter species.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the intracellular pH of Lp cells is significantly lower in monoculture than in co-culture with Acetobacter species.
evidence: The claim is based on pHluorin fluorescence measurements.

claim: The bulk growth rate of L. plantarum approaches zero as the pH approaches its final value of ~3.7.
source: The bulk growth rate approached zero (Figure 3B) as the pH approached its final value, explaining the differences in yield.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth rate measurements as a function of pH (Figure 3B).

claim: The highest growth rate of L. plantarum occurs at starting pH = 7.
source: Interestingly, the maximum growth rate was also pH-dependent (Figure 3C), with the highest growth rate at starting pH = 7.
evidence: The claim is supported by maximum growth rate measurements at various starting pH values (Figure 3C).

claim: The inhibition of growth in stationary phase of an L. plantarum monoculture is due to decreased intracellular and extracellular pH.
source: Given these findings, we hypothesized that the inhibition of growth in stationary phase of an Lp monoculture is due to the decreased intracellular and extracellular pH
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the pH and growth measurements.

claim: Ap releases L. plantarum's growth inhibition by raising intracellular and extracellular pH.
source: Given these findings, we hypothesized that the inhibition of growth in stationary phase of an Lp monoculture is due to the decreased intracellular and extracellular pH, and that Ap releases Lp's growth inhibition by raising intracellular and extracellular pH.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the pH and growth measurements.

claim: Almost no growth takes place in L. plantarum supernatant starting from pH = 3.77.
source: Almost no growth took place in supernatant starting from pH = 3.77, but we observed substantial growth (~20 fold increase in OD) of the bulk culture in supernatant raised to pH = 7 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth measurements in conditioned medium at different pH values (Figure 3D).

claim: Substantial growth (~20 fold increase in OD) of L. plantarum occurs in supernatant raised to pH = 7.
source: Almost no growth took place in supernatant starting from pH = 3.77, but we observed substantial growth (~20 fold increase in OD) of the bulk culture in supernatant raised to pH = 7 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth measurements in conditioned medium at different pH values (Figure 3D).

claim: The maximal growth rate of L. plantarum in pH-adjusted spent medium is lower than in fresh MRS.
source: As expected, the maximal growth rate was lower than in fresh MRS, presumably due to the partial depletion of nutrients (Figure 3D)
evidence: The claim is supported by growth rate measurements in conditioned versus fresh medium (Figure 3D).

claim: Addition of glucose to L. plantarum-conditioned medium supports faster growth, but only starting from neutral pH.
source: addition of glucose to the conditioned medium supported faster growth, but only starting from neutral pH (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth measurements in glucose-supplemented conditioned medium at different pH values (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Ap achieves a higher OD in Lp-conditioned medium than in fresh MRS.
source: When we diluted a saturated Ap culture in Lp-conditioned medium generated as above, Ap achieved an even higher OD than in fresh MRS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by OD measurements of Ap in conditioned versus fresh medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: pH is a driver of the growth advantages of L. plantarum in lag phase.
source: Thus, pH is a driver of the growth advantages of Lp in lag phase even in the absence of a net increase in cell number.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that pH adjustment shortens lag phase.

claim: The maximum growth rate is the same for L. plantarum monoculture and co-cultures with Ap, At, and Ai.
source: The maximum growth rate was the same for the Lp monoculture and co-cultures with Ap, At, and Ai, and slightly higher for co-cultures with Ao and Aa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by maximum growth rate measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: The maximum growth rate is slightly higher for L. plantarum co-cultures with Ao and Aa compared to monoculture.
source: The maximum growth rate was the same for the Lp monoculture and co-cultures with Ap, At, and Ai, and slightly higher for co-cultures with Ao and Aa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by maximum growth rate measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: There is a significant decrease in bulk lag time for all Acetobacter co-cultures with L. plantarum.
source: In agreement with these data, there was a significant decrease in bulk lag time for all the Acetobacter co-cultures (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by lag time measurements from growth curves (Figure 4A,B).

claim: The shorter lag phase in L. plantarum co-cultures is linked to tolerance to rifampin, opposite to the longer lag phase linked to E. coli tolerance to ampicillin.
source: Surprisingly, this shorter lag phase was linked to Lp tolerance to rifampin, opposite to the longer phase linked to E. coli tolerance to ampicillin (Brauner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous findings in E. coli.

claim: Ap, At, and Ai co-cultures have the largest lag decreases.
source: Ap, At, and Ai co-cultures had the largest lag decreases.
evidence: The claim is based on lag time measurements.

claim: Aa and Ao co-cultures have smaller, although still significant, decreases in lag time.
source: The Aa and Ao co-cultures had smaller, although still significant, decreases (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by lag time measurements (Figure 4A,B).

claim: Interspecies interactions can change the physiology of community members.
source: These data indicate that interspecies interactions can change the physiology of community members
evidence: The claim is a general conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Most L. plantarum cells in co-culture with Ap have grown by 1 h after spotting on agar pads.
source: In co-culture, most Lp cells were observed to have grown by 1 h after spotting, but in Lp monoculture, few cells were growing even after 2 h (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell imaging data (Figure 4E,F).

claim: In L. plantarum monoculture, few cells are growing even after 2 h on agar pads.
source: In co-culture, most Lp cells were observed to have grown by 1 h after spotting, but in Lp monoculture, few cells were growing even after 2 h (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell imaging data (Figure 4E,F).

claim: Ap cells do not grow during time-lapse imaging on agar pads.
source: Ap cells did not grow during the time of imaging (Figure 4F)
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell imaging data (Figure 4F).

claim: The reduced lag time in co-culture is due to L. plantarum's growth, not Ap's growth.
source: Ap cells did not grow during the time of imaging (Figure 4F), indicating that the reduced lag time was due to Lp's growth, in agreement with CFU/mL measurements from liquid cultures (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on single-cell imaging and CFU/mL measurements.

claim: Incubating L. plantarum monocultures for more than 48 h results in a dramatic increase in the duration of lag phase.
source: Incubating the Lp monocultures for more than 48 h resulted in a dramatic increase in the duration of lag phase, while reducing the culturing time shortened lag phase (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by lag time measurements from cultures grown for different durations (Figure 5A).

claim: Reducing the culturing time of L. plantarum monocultures shortens lag phase.
source: Incubating the Lp monocultures for more than 48 h resulted in a dramatic increase in the duration of lag phase, while reducing the culturing time shortened lag phase (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by lag time measurements from cultures grown for different durations (Figure 5A).

claim: The lag phase of a 20 h L. plantarum culture is slightly shorter than that of a co-culture.
source: Because lag phase in co-culture is slightly shorter than that of a 24 h monoculture (Figure 5A), we decided to match the lag time of a co-culture by growing a monoculture for 20 h from an initial OD = 0.02.
evidence: The claim is based on lag time measurements (Figure 5A).

claim: Neutralization of pH at 40 h elicits longer protection against rifampin than neutralization at 30 h.
source: Neutralization of pH in Lp monocultures at 40 h of growth (to mimic Lp+Aa co-cultures) elicits longer protection against rifampin than neutralization at 30 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements after pH neutralization at different time points (Figure 5F).

claim: A small increase in pH (from 3.85 to 4.5) at 30 h provides protection comparable to complete neutralization.
source: A small increase in pH (from 3.85 to 4.5) at 30 h (to mimic Lp+Ao co-cultures) provides protection comparable to complete neutralization.
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements after partial pH increase (Figure 5F).

claim: All pH shifts induce higher tolerance compared to control cultures that underwent the same protocol but whose pH was maintained.
source: All pH shifts induced higher tolerance compared to control cultures that underwent the same protocol but whose pH was maintained (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements comparing pH-shifted and control cultures (Figure 5F).

claim: pH changes drive changes in both the exit from stationary phase and tolerance of L. plantarum to rifampin.
source: Taken together, these experiments establish that pH changes drive changes in both the exit from stationary phase and tolerance of Lp to rifampin.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the pH manipulation experiments.

claim: At concentrations above the MIC, the 48 h L. plantarum culture shows no changes in CFU/mL after 24 h of erythromycin treatment.
source: While both cultures had the same MIC in erythromycin (0.078 µg/mL, Figure 5G), at concentrations above the MIC, the 48 h culture showed no changes in CFU/mL after 24 h of erythromycin treatment
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements (Figure 5G).

claim: The 20 h L. plantarum culture has a reduction of ~10 fold in CFU/mL after 24 h of erythromycin treatment at supra-MIC concentrations.
source: the 20 h culture had a reduction of ~10 fold in CFU/mL (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements (Figure 5G).

claim: L. plantarum cells are typically tolerant to erythromycin but killing is accelerated under conditions that make them tolerant to rifampin.
source: This result suggests that Lp cells are typically tolerant to erythromycin but killing is accelerated under conditions that make them tolerant to rifampin.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the opposite effects of culture age on rifampin versus erythromycin tolerance.

claim: Cells from a 20 h L. plantarum culture die significantly more rapidly than cells from a 48-hr-old culture when exposed to 2 µg/mL erythromycin.
source: Cells from a 20 h culture died significantly more rapidly than cells from a 48-hr-old culture (Figure 5H)
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course CFU/mL measurements (Figure 5H).

claim: The differences in survival to erythromycin between 20 h and 48 h cultures are explained by erythromycin tolerance.
source: Cells from a 20 h culture died significantly more rapidly than cells from a 48-hr-old culture (Figure 5H), indicating that the differences in survival (Figure 5G) are explained by erythromycin tolerance.
evidence: The claim is based on the time-to-kill measurements.

claim: Increasing the pH of an L. plantarum monoculture at 30 h and exposing it to 2 µg/mL erythromycin after 18 h increases the rate of killing similar to a 20 h culture.
source: Further, increasing the pH of an Lp monoculture at 30 h and then exposing it after an additional 18 h of growth to 2 µg/mL erythromycin in fresh medium had an increase in the rate of killing that was similar to that achieved with a 20 h culture (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course CFU/mL measurements (Figure 5H).

claim: The effects of changing the growth status of a culture on antibiotic response are not limited to rifampin.
source: These results highlight that the effects of changing the growth status of a culture on antibiotic response are not limited to rifampin and—as in the case of erythromycin—can be opposite.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the erythromycin experiments.

claim: The effects of changing the growth status of a culture on antibiotic response can be opposite for different antibiotics.
source: These results highlight that the effects of changing the growth status of a culture on antibiotic response are not limited to rifampin and—as in the case of erythromycin—can be opposite.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparing rifampin and erythromycin results.

claim: The generality of the pH-based mechanism should be tested broadly in other contexts.
source: Moreover, these findings could have important implications for human health, for example in the context of Lactobacillus-dominated vaginal microbiotas (Boris and Barbés, 2000), hence their generality should be tested broadly in other contexts.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: L. plantarum cells in monoculture rapidly die when exposed to high concentrations of rifampin.
source: Lp cells in monoculture rapidly died, while Lp cells in co-cultures showed close to 100% survival for extended periods (Figures 1E and 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course CFU/mL measurements (Figures 1E and 5E).

claim: L. plantarum cells in co-cultures show close to 100% survival for extended periods when exposed to high concentrations of rifampin.
source: Lp cells in monoculture rapidly died, while Lp cells in co-cultures showed close to 100% survival for extended periods (Figures 1E and 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course CFU/mL measurements (Figures 1E and 5E).

claim: The time and magnitude of pH change affect the kinetics of killing but not the size of the surviving population.
source: Furthermore, the time and magnitude of pH change affected the kinetics of killing but not the size of the surviving population (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU/mL measurements with different pH manipulation protocols (Figure 5E and F).

claim: The observed behaviors in L. plantarum contrast with the stereotypical rapid decrease in viability with a small subpopulation of surviving cells observed in persistence.
source: These behaviors contrast with the stereotypical rapid decrease in viability, with a small subpopulation of surviving cells, observed in persistence.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with known persistence phenotypes.

claim: At high doses and late time points, L. plantarum cell counts were below the limit of detection.
source: At high doses and late time points, cell counts were below our limit of detection and therefore we cannot rule out that, in addition to tolerance, pH changes in stationary phase could also modulate persistence.
evidence: The claim is stated as a limitation of the measurements.

claim: pH changes in stationary phase could potentially modulate persistence in addition to tolerance.
source: At high doses and late time points, cell counts were below our limit of detection and therefore we cannot rule out that, in addition to tolerance, pH changes in stationary phase could also modulate persistence.
evidence: The claim is speculative due to measurement limitations.

claim: Killing retardation due to pH increase in stationary phase is at least an order of magnitude longer than the change in lag time.
source: Moreover, although tolerance to erythromycin was associated with a longer lag phase (Figures 3E and 5A,H), killing retardation was at least an order of magnitude longer than the change in lag time (Figure 5A,H)
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of lag time changes and killing kinetics.

claim: Tolerance is not determined by an elongation of lag phase alone, in contrast to the effects of ampicillin on E. coli.
source: indicating that tolerance is not determined by an elongation of lag phase alone, in contrast to the effects of ampicillin on E. coli (Fridman et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous findings in E. coli.

claim: The opposite behaviors of L. plantarum to rifampin and erythromycin upon pH changes suggest that tolerance is more complex than previously thought.
source: The opposite behaviors of Lp to rifampin and erythromycin upon pH changes suggest that tolerance is more complex than previously thought, and should motivate future investigations into the physiological and genetic basis of tolerance.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion and recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Several genetic factors that increase time to killing have been identified in E. coli, including toxin-antitoxin modules such as hipBA.
source: Several genetic factors that increase time to killing have been identified in E. coli, including toxin-antitoxin modules such as hipBA (Rotem et al., 2010) that induce the stringent response and thus cause transient growth arrest.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rotem et al., 2010.

claim: Toxin-antitoxin modules such as hipBA induce the stringent response and cause transient growth arrest.
source: Several genetic factors that increase time to killing have been identified in E. coli, including toxin-antitoxin modules such as hipBA (Rotem et al., 2010) that induce the stringent response and thus cause transient growth arrest.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rotem et al., 2010.

claim: Metabolic interactions alter the physiological state of L. plantarum during late stationary phase by changing the environmental pH.
source: In Lp co-culture with Acetobacter species, metabolic interactions alter the physiological state of Lp during late stationary phase by changing the environmental pH (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on measurements of pH and growth in co-cultures (Figure 2).

claim: Whether the stringent response could be a major factor in the increased tolerance to rifampin in L. plantarum is unclear due to the surprising connection with decreased lag.
source: In the case of Lp, whether the stringent response could be a major factor in the increased tolerance to rifampin is unclear due to the surprising connection with decreased lag.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the unexpected relationship between lag and tolerance.

claim: The pH in stationary phase can affect many factors, such as the chemistry of extracellular metabolites and macromolecules as well as the surface of the cell.
source: The pH in stationary phase can affect many factors, such as the chemistry of extracellular metabolites and macromolecules as well as the surface of the cell (Peters et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peters et al., 2016.

claim: All antibiotic sensitivity assays were performed at a starting pH of 7.
source: Importantly, our assays of antibiotic sensitivities were all performed at a starting pH of 7.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Shifts in extracellular pH can lead to buffered drops in cytoplasmic pH.
source: Nonetheless, shifts in extracellular pH can lead to buffered drops in cytoplasmic pH (Choi and Groisman, 2016; Olsen et al., 2002) that can be regulated (Chakraborty et al., 2015) or result from internalization of low-pKa species such as short-chain fatty acids (Ricke, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Choi and Groisman, 2016, Olsen et al., 2002, Chakraborty et al., 2015, and Ricke, 2003.

claim: Changes in pH can be regulated.
source: Nonetheless, shifts in extracellular pH can lead to buffered drops in cytoplasmic pH (Choi and Groisman, 2016; Olsen et al., 2002) that can be regulated (Chakraborty et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chakraborty et al., 2015.

claim: Changes in pH can result from internalization of low-pKa species such as short-chain fatty acids.
source: Nonetheless, shifts in extracellular pH can lead to buffered drops in cytoplasmic pH (Choi and Groisman, 2016; Olsen et al., 2002) that can be regulated (Chakraborty et al., 2015) or result from internalization of low-pKa species such as short-chain fatty acids (Ricke, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ricke, 2003.

claim: How pH-related factors affect non-polycationic antibiotics such as rifampin remains to be determined.
source: How these factors affect non-polycationic antibiotics such as rifampin remains to be determined
evidence: The claim identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Neither rifampin nor erythromycin have ionizable functional groups with pKas in the pH range achieved in the cultures.
source: neither of the ionizable functional groups of rifampin (pKas 1.7 and 7.9 Maggi et al., 1966) nor erythromycin (pKa 8.88 McFarland et al., 1997) have pKas in the pH range achieved in our cultures (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of antibiotic pKa values with measured pH ranges.

claim: Protonation changes in target macromolecules could lead to protection against antibiotics, although this would be expected to change the MIC.
source: Protonation changes in target macromolecules could also lead to protection against antibiotics, although we would expect a subsequent change in MIC, contrary to our findings (Figures 1 and 5).
evidence: The claim is speculative but argues against this mechanism based on the lack of MIC change.

claim: Lactobacillus and Acetobacter form a recurrent community and may have evolved to sense and benefit from each other's presence.
source: One major factor influencing the Lactobacillus-Acetobacter interaction is that these organisms form a recurrent community and may therefore have evolved to sense and benefit from each other's presence.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the ecological context.

claim: Further experiments are needed to uncover the molecular mechanisms that link growth state and susceptibility to antibiotics in Lactobacillus species, other non-model organisms, and microbial communities.
source: Further experiments are needed to uncover the molecular mechanisms that link growth state and susceptibility to antibiotics in Lactobacillus species, other non-model organisms, and microbial communities.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation for future research.

claim: It remains to be established whether lag time and tolerance are causally linked or coupled to some global variable.
source: In addition, although we consistently observed related shifts in lag phase and tolerance (Figures 3 and 5), it remains to be established whether lag time and tolerance are causally linked or coupled to some global variable.
evidence: The claim identifies a limitation and future research direction.

claim: The opposite connections with rifampin and erythromycin tolerance underscore the complexity of the link between growth and antibiotic action.
source: The opposite connections with rifampin and erythromycin tolerance underscore the complexity of the link between growth and antibiotic action.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the contrasting results with different antibiotics.

claim: Changes in growth may lead to changes in the levels and activity of antibiotic molecular targets.
source: Changes in growth may lead to changes in the levels and activity of these antibiotics' molecular targets.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential mechanisms.

claim: The molecular mechanisms that lead to death downstream of the antibiotic target could be a function of the growth state of the cell.
source: Moreover, the molecular mechanisms that lead to death downstream of the antibiotic target could be a function of the growth state of the cell.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential mechanisms.

claim: Bacterial interactions can elicit changes in antibiotic sensitivity by changing cellular physiology or interfering with antibiotic action directly or indirectly.
source: Previous work has shown that bacterial interactions can elicit changes in antibiotic sensitivity by changing cellular physiology or interfering with antibiotic action directly or indirectly (Adamowicz et al., 2018; Radlinski et al., 2017; Sorg et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Adamowicz et al., 2018, Radlinski et al., 2017, and Sorg et al., 2016.

claim: A myriad of intra- and extracellular variables are subject to the composition and dynamics of the ecosystems that bacteria inhabit.
source: In principle, a myriad of intra- and extracellular variables are subject to the composition and dynamics of the ecosystems that bacteria inhabit
evidence: The claim is a general statement about microbial ecology.

claim: Microbial communities within animal hosts can elicit changes in environmental variables both locally and globally.
source: and microbial communities within animal hosts can elicit changes in environmental variables both locally and globally.
evidence: The claim is a general statement about host-microbiome interactions.

claim: The microaerobic and anaerobic microenvironments of the fly and human gastrointestinal tracts enable the growth of short chain fatty acid producers.
source: Specifically, the microaerobic and anaerobic microenvironments of the fly (Obadia et al., 2017) and human gastrointestinal tracts enable the growth of short chain fatty acid producers.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Obadia et al., 2017 and general knowledge.

claim: The consequences of the accumulation of short chain fatty acids and other small molecules on microenvironments, as well as their effect on bacterial physiology and antibiotic treatment efficacy in vivo, have yet to be systematically explored.
source: The consequences of the accumulation of these short chain fatty acids and other small molecules on microenvironments, as well as their effect on bacterial physiology and antibiotic treatment efficacy in vivo, have yet to be systematically explored.
evidence: The claim identifies a knowledge gap and future research direction.

claim: The findings linking short chain fatty acid metabolism, growth, and antibiotic action in commensal microbes from the fruit fly gut open the door to studying these phenomena in a model organism.
source: Our findings linking short chain fatty acid metabolism, growth, and antibiotic action in commensal microbes from the fruit fly gut opens the door to studying these phenomena in a model organism.
evidence: The claim is a forward-looking statement about the implications of the study.

claim: The human gut microbiome comprises hundreds of bacterial species.
source: While the human gut microbiome comprises hundreds of bacterial species
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The simplicity of the Drosophila gut microbiota makes the fruit fly a powerful model for host-microbiome interactions.
source: the simplicity of the Drosophila gut microbiota (Wong et al., 2011), the genetic tractability of Drosophila, and the fact that ~ 65% of human disease-causing genes have homologs in the Drosophila genome (Ugur et al., 2016), make the fruit fly a powerful model for host-microbiome interactions (Douglas, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wong et al., 2011, Ugur et al., 2016, and Douglas, 2018.

claim: The genetic tractability of Drosophila makes the fruit fly a powerful model for host-microbiome interactions.
source: the simplicity of the Drosophila gut microbiota (Wong et al., 2011), the genetic tractability of Drosophila, and the fact that ~ 65% of human disease-causing genes have homologs in the Drosophila genome (Ugur et al., 2016), make the fruit fly a powerful model for host-microbiome interactions (Douglas, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and general knowledge.

claim: The results emphasize the need to probe the action of antibiotics in complex and varied conditions.
source: Our results also emphasize the need to probe the action of antibiotics – as well as other drugs that are thought not to target microbial growth (Maier et al., 2018) – in complex and varied conditions (Beppler et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the study's findings, supported by citations to Maier et al., 2018 and Beppler et al., 2017.

claim: The findings highlight the utility of studying growth physiology in co-cultures in the absence of antibiotics for uncovering novel mechanisms of community-encoded protection against antibiotics.
source: Furthermore, our findings highlight the utility of studying growth physiology in co-cultures in the absence of antibiotics for uncovering novel mechanisms of community-encoded protection against antibiotics.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion about the methodological approach of the study.
